Futures are leading a rebound this morning after a broad risk-off session. ES is 7648.0 (+0.43%), NQ +0.17% and Dow futures +0.40%. That follows a prior close of S&P 500 7592.4 (-0.35%), Nasdaq -0.39% and Russell 2000 -1.66%, so small caps did most of the damage. VIX eased to 17.79 from 18.7. The bigger story is still bonds. The US 10Y is 5.1433% (+1.6bp) and the 30Y is 5.4731% (+2.1bp), while the 2Y slipped 1.4bp to 4.8674%: a bear steepener. It is global: JGB 10Y +5.8bp to 2.871%, Bund +3.7bp, Gilt +3.8bp. Brent is up 1.13% to 96.9 as the Iran stalemate keeps Hormuz effectively closed. Two credit stories need attention. First, HY contagion: the Caa–B gap is 780bp, at the 99.2nd percentile of 5 years and nearly double its 420bp 5y average, and it widened +20bp on the week and +205bp over 3 months. The FRED CCC–B measure is 983bp at the 99.1st percentile. So far the rot is NOT spreading up the ladder. Single-B (-26bp 1w) and Ba (-28bp 1w) tightened, the B–Ba gap of 122bp sits near its 128.8bp average, and IG is 86bp. One thing to watch: the 63-day Caa/B correlation has risen to 0.65 from 0.33 three months ago, though it is still below its 0.69 5y median. This is descriptive, not a signal. Second, the AI backstop: CoreWeave 5Y CDS fell 88.5bp on the day and 237bp on the week to ~1,076bp, which is 118.6bp inside the 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record. But it is still 624bp above the 452bp June low, so 84% of the run-up is still in the price. Nvidia CDS dipped 2.1bp to 141.7bp, and CoreWeave notes rallied ~5–6.5 points on the week. The market is partly buying Nvidia's backstop of the neoclouds, not fully. On tech, the phase model keeps the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 27 days after the peak, with the basket -14.41% vs -18.9% for 2000 on the same day. One signpost has triggered: 57.1% of basket names are >20% off their highs, above the 50% line. SOX is -28.2% from its 52w high, close to the -30% line. The relief-rally conditions are on, which fits this morning's bounce. Sentiment is fragile but not panicked.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.92 vol points (84th percentile of the 68 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 98.4 (71th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 89bp (flatter by 1bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (101bp above today).

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 43 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 66/100 — Sticky and slowly broadening, not re-accelerating in wages. The trimmed and median core measures are mostly above their historical median and drifting higher: Median CPI 2.8 (rising), 16% Trimmed-Mean CPI 2.9 (rising) and Core Sticky CPI 3.0595 (rising). Median PCE (2.67) and Trimmed-Mean PCE (2.26) are flat. The computed Core-Trend Sub-Score (rendered separately) puts this in the upper-middle of history. Breadth is split: 16.6% of the PCE basket is rising >10% and 10.2% is rising 5–10%, while 25.6% is falling. The hot tail is concentrated in flexible prices (Flexible CPI 6.201), which is consistent with oil and Hormuz. Wages are not the driver (AHE 3.1, ECI 0.8). Markets are not pricing persistence (5y breakeven 2.3287, 1y 2.0683), so there is upside risk to breakevens if oil stays near $97 Brent. Persistence score is an analyst estimate.

Today looks like the early bust phase, not the March-2000 peak. Equity froth has deflated: Nasdaq trailing P/E 39.52x is 15% of the way to the 2000 peak, the Nasdaq is only 0.9% above its 200DMA (2%), and SOX P/E is 36.04x (40%). Late-cycle catalysts are mixed: the 2s10s is at 71% and the PMI rollovers at 1%/13%. Credit tightness reads beyond 2000 conditions (IG 128%, Baa–10Y 175%). Among bear-market signposts, VIX complacency (175%) and loose NFCI (148%) contrast with deeply bearish AAII (-20.6, 0%). The phase model puts the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm) on day 27, at -14.41% vs -18.9% for the 2000 basket on the same day. Model odds at 6 months: P1 0.517, P2 0.273, P3 0.101, P4 0.109. The model puts the chance of ever reaching Phase 2+ within 12 months at 0.557. These are model estimates, not certainties. The breadth signpost has triggered (57.1% of names >20% off highs). The 6m P2+P3 odds rose 1.1pp vs the prior run, with no phase change. Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (40x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analog says the danger is not today's valuations but the transition from Phase 1 to Phase 2, when credit starts to widen. The model's credit signposts are still far away: HY 312bp vs a 448bp trigger and Baa–10Y 136.3bp vs 195.07bp. Two AI-credit indicators are closer: CoreWeave CDS sits 118.6bp below its record, and SOX is 1.8pp from its -30% line. Nvidia's Nov 17 print is the near-term swing factor for both. The relief-rally conditions are on (VIX spike-and-turn with calm credit). Historically, about 47.4% of such rallies were traps (typical trap ~17.5 days, +10.7%), against real rallies of ~106.5 days and +32.4%. Treat the current bounce as unproven.

Odds the volatility-washout conditions line up within a week: 75%; within two weeks: 75%. Rallies of 8%+ that start in this phase: 47% later fail below their starting low (median 18 trading days, +11%); the rest become recoveries (median 106 days, +32%). Descriptive, not a signal.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

⚔️Iran War

The war is in a 'no war, no peace' stalemate with no ceasefire in force. The interim deal collapsed on 8 July. Iran has sent seven conditions through Qatari mediators, including lifting the US naval blockade of its ports, ending sanctions, guaranteeing an end to strikes and a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon. It is awaiting a formal US reply and has offered to shorten some implementation timelines from seven days to two. On Nov 11, parliament speaker Ghalibaf said the Strait of Hormuz will 'never return' to its pre-war status and cited an Iran–Oman understanding to oversee it. Trump said 'we don't need a deal with Iran,' while mediators work on a framework that would trade an end to Iranian attacks in Hormuz for lifting the blockade. Commercial vessels have hit mines or been struck over the past week, and the US carried out limited strikes on Qeshm Island on Nov 2 and Nov 6. Market read: this keeps a risk premium in crude (Brent 96.9, +1.13%) and in flexible inflation.

Sources: Al Jazeera — Hormuz Strait will 'never return' to pre-war status, Ghalibaf says (Nov 11, 2026) · Al Jazeera — 'No war, no peace': Can Iran break the deadlock with the US? 🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at the next meeting (inference). Warsh has favored lower rates on productivity grounds, but he needs a committee majority. Some members reportedly want to signal that a hike is as likely as a cut. With core PCE at 3.12115 and the 10Y at 5.14%, a cut now looks hard to push through. This is inferred, not stated by Warsh.

~1 YEAR

A gradual regime change rather than aggressive easing (inference). Expect output from his five task forces on communications, the balance sheet, the inflation framework, data and productivity. Expect less forward guidance (he declined to submit his own SEP projections) and a slow, committee-approved bias toward a smaller balance sheet. Analysts doubt any shrinkage will be meaningful. Cuts are possible if productivity and inflation data allow.

At his first meeting as chair (June 2026), Warsh declined to submit SEP forecasts and launched five review task forces, per Cato. His long-held view favors a smaller Fed balance sheet, but changes need committee approval and gradual implementation. Pepperstone judged significant shrinkage unlikely. PIMCO's pre-confirmation baseline was that he could assemble the votes for cuts, but other coverage notes resistance on the committee. Flag: the near-term and one-year calls above are analyst inference from his record. No November-2026 Warsh statement was found in this run.

Sources: Cato — Trump picked Kevin Warsh to cut rates · PIMCO — Under a Warsh Fed, expect a thoughtful policy approach · Pepperstone — What a Warsh Fed might look like · Gulf Times — Warsh's Fed regime change may require patience, consensus · MarketScreener — A regime change: Kevin Warsh, the man who wants to revolutionize the Fed
